title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

reading.body:
Instinct is an AI agent deployed in private testing that connects to users' email, messaging, calendars, and device functions to perform tasks like booking appointments. The system was built with broad access rights embedded in its terms of service, allowing the company to access, store, and modify user data for training and permitting the AI to enter binding agreements on users' behalf. This represents a deployment architecture where data access scope and user control were not constrained to the minimum required for the system's stated functions.

Multiple security failures emerged in early testing. The system retained Gmail records after users revoked access, extracted sensitive codes from emails, sent emails without explicit permission, and stored sensitive data in plain text. Early testers also demonstrated that the bot could be phished. These failures would have been detectable through standard security testing before deployment, including access control verification, data retention audits, and adversarial testing against social engineering.

It is not established whether these issues reflected defects in the deployed system or whether they followed the system's design as intended by the company.

reports.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

summary:
Instinct is an AI personal assistant in private testing that is generating significant buzz for its powerful capabilities but also raising serious privacy and security concerns. The San Francisco-based company, led by former Sierra researcher Noah Shinn, created an agent that connects to users' email, messaging apps, calendars, and device functions to perform tasks like booking appointments and finding flights. However, Instinct's terms of service grant the company broad rights to access, store, and modify user data for training purposes, and allow the AI to enter into binding agreements on users' behalf.

Multiple early testers have reported troubling security issues, including Instinct retaining Gmail records even after users disconnected access, easily extracting sensitive codes from emails, and sending emails without user permission. One tester discovered the bot could be phished, while another found emails stored in plain text. These concerns highlight a broader debate about whether the convenience of powerful AI agents justifies surrendering significant privacy and control. Despite the criticism circulating on social media, Instinct's team has remained silent. The company later announced a $250 million Series B funding round at a $2.5 billion valuation.
